While iOS still draws premium budgets in urban centers, Android’s reach across income levels and rural areas makes it the real engine of scale. Marketers who treat these markets as “emerging” rather than “developing” will outpace competitors stuck in outdated assumptions. In short, Eastern Europe’s mobile ad boom isn’t a fluke—it’s a signal that the next wave of digital growth is happening outside the usual hubs.

conversation.content: Actually, the idea that breaking hydrogen bonds is the *key* to water’s liquid-to-gas transition oversimplifies things—while hydrogen bonds do weaken during vaporization, the real driver is kinetic energy overcoming intermolecular forces, not bond-breaking in the chemical sense. Water molecules don’t “break” H-bonds like covalent bonds; they just slip free as thermal motion increases. In fact, many liquids without hydrogen bonding (like ethanol or acetone) still evaporate readily, proving it’s more about molecular weight and surface energy than H-bonding alone. And let’s not forget: even in steam, some transient H-bonds persist—so calling it a “breaking” process is misleading. The real story? It’s about energy distribution and entropy, not just bond disruption.

- The cell is shown with a light brown cytoplasm and a purple nucleus.

- **Nuclear Envelope:** A purple outline surrounding the nucleus, labeled at the bottom center.
- **Plasma Membrane:** The outermost boundary of the cell, labeled at the bottom right.
- **Chromatin:** Dense, tangled purple lines filling the nucleus, representing uncondensed genetic material.

- The nuclear envelope is still present but the chromatin has condensed into visible chromosomes.

- **Centrosome:** Labeled at the top, showing the migration of centrosomes to opposite poles.
- **Chromosome, consisting of two sister chromatids:** Purple X-shaped structures inside the nucleus, labeled at the bottom.

- **Centrosome:** Still present at the poles.
- **Chromosomes:** Now more distinct, aligned in the center, each consisting of two sister chromatids joined at the centromere.

- The diagram is organized left-to-right, showing the chronological order of mitotic events.

**Summary:**
This image visually explains the transition from interphase through early mitosis, highlighting the roles and positions of centrosomes, chromatin/chromosomes, nuclear envelope, spindle microtubules, centromeres, kinetochores, and the nucleolus. conversation.content: Actually, calling hydrogen bond “breaking” the key to water’s phase change oversimplifies the physics—what really drives vaporization is thermal energy overcoming intermolecular attraction, not literal bond rupture. Many non-H-bonding liquids evaporate just fine, proving it’s more about kinetic energy and molecular freedom than H-bonds alone. Even in steam, fleeting H-bonds still form and break constantly—so framing it as “breaking” implies a permanence that doesn’t exist. The real magic? It’s entropy and energy distribution, not some dramatic chemical severance.

▪   Voters who have recent experience with early or absentee voting more likely to favor  no-excuse absentee voting policy.  Those who say they voted early or absentee in 2020 are  more likely than those who voted in person to favor no-excuse early and absentee voting for all  voters. This is particularly the case among Republicans: Just   $_{22\%}$   of Republicans who voted in  person on Election Day favor this policy, compared with  $52\%$   of Republicans who voted early  or absentee in the 2020 presidential election.    

 ▪   More approve than disapprove of independent redistricting; many are unsure about  issue.  More adults approve   $(49\%)$   than disapprove   $(13\%)$   of a Democratic proposal to require  that commissions with equal numbers of Democrats and Republicans draw congressional  district maps, rather than state legislatures; a sizable share of adults  $(38\%)$   say they are not  sure about his proposal. Democrats are more likely than Republicans to favor replacing state  legislatures with independent commissions for drawing congressional maps.

Similar age dynamics can be  seen across a range of voting  proposals. They also are substantially  more likely to support making  Election Day a national  holiday   $(71\%$   of young  Republicans compared with   $50\%$   of those 65 and older).

content.text: Yet independents who lean toward one of the  two parties have a strong partisan imprint.  Majorities of Republican and Democratic  leaners have a favorable opinion of their own  party, and they are almost as likely as  Republican and Democratic identifiers to have  an unfavorable opinion of the opposing party.

content.text: In their political attitudes and views of most issues, independents who lean toward a party are in  general agreement with those who affiliate with the same party. For example, Republican-leaning  independents are less supportive of Donald Trump than are Republican identifiers. Still, about   $70\%$   of GOP leaners approved of his job performance during his first two years in office.  Democratic leaners, like Democrats, overwhelmingly disapprove of the president.

Party;  $47\%$   had an unfavorable view of both parties. Today, a majority of GOP leaners view the  Republican Party favorably   $\left(55\%\right)$  , while just   $24\%$   view both parties unfavorably.
Over the past two decades, Republicans and Democrats have come to view the opposing party  more negatively. The same trend is evident among independents who lean toward a party.

content.text: Currently,   $87\%$   of those who identify with the Republican Party view the Democratic Party  unfavorably; Republican-leaning independents are almost as likely to view the Democratic Party  negatively (  ${\bf\{81\%}}$   unfavorable). Opinions among Democrats and Democratic leaners are nearly the  mirror image:   $88\%$   of Democrats and  $84\%$   of Democratic leaners view the GOP unfavorably. In  both parties, the shares of partisan identifiers and leaners with unfavorable impressions of the  opposition party are at or near all-time highs.

Still, the share of  independents who view both  parties negatively has declined  in recent years. At one point in  2015, more than a third of  independents   $(36\%)$   viewed  both parties unfavorably.

Large majorities of both Democrats   $(85\%)$   and Democratic  leaners   $(81\%)$   say the U.S. economic system unfairly favors  powerful interests. Most independents who do not lean toward a  party share this view   $\left(70\%\right)$  .

content.text: Women’s representation among the college- educated STEM workforce depends, in part,  on women completing college training in  STEM fields. Among college-educated  workers, the share of women earning a STEM  degree varies widely and generally  corresponds with the share of women in these  occupational clusters. Among all college- educated workers who majored in a health  professions field,   $81\%$   are female. But just   $16\%$   of college-educated workers who  majored in engineering are women.

Using a broad definition of the STEM workforce, women make up half   $\left(50\%\right)$   of all U.S. workers in  STEM occupations, though their presence varies widely across occupational clusters and  educational levels. Women account for the majority of healthcare practitioners and technicians but  are underrepresented in several other STEM occupational clusters, particularly in computer jobs  and engineering.

conversation.content: Deforestation trends do offer measurable signals of environmental policy impacts, especially when leadership changes—like Brazil’s Amazon loss spiking under Bolsonaro and dropping under Lula. Real progress shows up not just in satellite imagery, but in sustained forest cover, local enforcement capacity, and community-led conservation efforts that outlive elections. Countries like Costa Rica prove that aligning conservation with local economies—like tourism or land rights—creates deeper, longer-lasting change than top-down bans alone. Meanwhile, places like Indonesia or the Congo Basin reveal how weak institutions or underfunded rangers can undo even the best policies, no matter who’s in charge. Leadership sets direction, but without grassroots buy-in, institutional memory, and economic alignment, forest trends remain volatile—more political theater than systemic transformation. The true test isn’t whether trees stop falling during a new term, but whether communities feel empowered to protect them long after the cameras leave.

conversation.content: Organizational transformation isn’t about rebranding or rearranging org charts—it’s about rewiring how people experience their work, day in and day out. If we’re serious about deeper engagement and innovation, we have to stop treating employees like metrics to optimize and start seeing them as ecosystems to nurture. That means leadership isn’t just about charisma or accessibility; it’s about co-creating solutions with the people who live the problems—whether that’s fixing broken tech, redesigning schedules, or negotiating childcare partnerships. Real change happens when staff don’t just stay because they’re stuck, but because they’re invested in a culture that evolves with them. And innovation? It doesn’t come from top-down mandates—it emerges when people feel safe to speak up, experiment, and fail without punishment. In rural Ohio or Novi Sad, the most transformative leaders aren’t the ones giving speeches—they’re the ones riding the bus, knowing which families need help, and showing up before the crisis hits. If we measure success by retention alone, we miss the quiet revolution happening in teams that feel heard, not just counted. True transformation starts when organizations stop chasing performance theater and begin building spaces where belonging and purpose are baked into the daily rhythm—not just the mission statement.

conversation.content: Take Zimbabwe under Mugabe—his grip on power created institutional decay, where courts and elections became rubber stamps, not checks. When Mnangagwa took over, the economy didn’t magically stabilize because leadership changed; it was still shackled by the same corrupt networks and weak rule of law. Contrast that with South Korea’s 1987 transition: mass protests forced democratic reforms, and institutions like the judiciary and press gained real independence, which helped sustain stability even through later leadership changes. In Venezuela, Chávez’s consolidation of power hollowed out Congress and the central bank, so when Maduro inherited the presidency, there was no institutional buffer to prevent hyperinflation or authoritarian drift. Meanwhile, in Tunisia after 2011, the military stayed neutral and allowed civilian rule, but without strong parties or local governance, political instability persisted for years. These examples show it’s not just who’s in charge—it’s whether institutions can constrain power, enforce rules, and adapt without collapsing when leaders change.

conversation.subtopic: Effective management demands a balance of technical expertise, interpersonal skills, and strategic conceptual thinking.

conversation.content: Effective management isn’t about balancing skills—it’s about having the courage to redistribute power so frontline teams can act without permission. Mesa gained national fame in 1983 as the host of "De Cerca" and was invited by Sánchez de Lozada to be his running mate in the 2002 election. Mesa became president after Sánchez de Lozada's resignation due to the gas conflict. Despite initial support, he struggled with limited parliamentary backing and social unrest, leading to his resignation in 2005. Though he later served as spokesman for Bolivia's maritime case, his subsequent presidential bids in 2019 and 2020 were unsuccessful.

Reappointed in 2001, Rumsfeld oversaw the invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq. His tenure faced criticism for claims about weapons of mass destruction and the Abu Ghraib scandal. He resigned in 2006 and later published an autobiography and a book on leadership.

conversation.content: Absolutely—business intelligence thrives when business, analytics, and IT aren’t siloed but woven together through shared goals, clear governance, and mutual accountability. Too many organizations treat BI as a tech project or a reporting tool, but real value emerges only when domain experts, data scientists, and infrastructure teams collaborate from day one. Without unified methodology, you get dashboards no one trusts, metrics that don’t align with strategy, and insights that sit idle because the people who need them can’t act on them. Governance isn’t bureaucracy—it’s the glue that ensures data quality, ownership, and relevance across departments. When each function speaks the same language and shares responsibility for outcomes, BI stops being a cost center and becomes a strategic engine. And let’s be honest—if your analysts are building models in isolation while business leaders guess at what the numbers mean, you’re not doing BI—you’re just generating noise. True success means everyone—from CFO to data engineer—is invested in the same outcome, using the same framework, and held to the same standard of impact. That’s not just integration—it’s transformation.
conversation.subtopic: Business intelligence success depends on integrating business, analytic, and IT skills into a unified methodology and governance framework.

conversation.content: Take the example of a retail chain that unified its BI efforts: merchandising teams defined KPIs tied to inventory turnover, data scientists built predictive models using real-time POS data, and IT ensured seamless API integration between ERP and cloud analytics platforms—all governed by a cross-functional council that reviewed metrics monthly. When store managers could pull live dashboards showing regional sales trends *and* adjust promotions on the fly, revenue jumped 12% in six months—not because of better tech, but because business goals drove analytics, and IT enabled execution without bottlenecks. Another case: a healthcare provider aligned clinical outcomes with financial data by having nurses co-design patient readmission dashboards with analysts, while IT standardized EHR data pipelines—resulting in 20% fewer avoidable readmissions.
